name: Vienna
distance_from_hq_phrase: Vienna is 10-15 minutes from our home base in Fairfax
geographic_anchor_paragraph: Vienna, VA sits at an interesting electrical crossroads. The town runs roughly between the Wolf Trap area to the west, the Tysons-edge to the east, Hunter Mill Road as its southern spine, and the Maple Avenue corridor at the center.
audience_descriptor: Residential homeowners in Vienna, VA and surrounding Northern Fairfax County neighborhoods including Vienna Woods, Hunter Mill, Tysons-edge, and Wolf Trap.

other_areas_paragraph: Outside Vienna, we serve Fairfax, McLean, Oakton, Tysons, Burke, Annandale, Falls Church, and the rest of Fairfax County. We also cover DC and Montgomery County, MD (Rockville, Bethesda, Chevy Chase, Potomac).

housing_patterns.title: 1950s-1970s split-levels & ranches
housing_patterns.neighborhood_examples: Vienna Woods, Country Club area, neighborhoods near Westwood
housing_patterns.context_paragraph: Built with 100-amp panels and circuits sized for the appliances of the era — toaster, fridge, color TV, a window unit if you were lucky. Fast-forward to 2026: induction range, central AC, two refrigerators, a tankless water heater, and an EV charger in the garage. Modern load patterns overwhelm circuits the original builder never planned for.
housing_patterns.symptoms: persistent breaker trips, warm outlets, dimming lights when large appliances start.

housing_patterns.title: 1970s-1990s colonials & traditionals
housing_patterns.neighborhood_examples: Hunter Mill District, Vienna proper, north of Maple Avenue
housing_patterns.context_paragraph: 200-amp service but wired with the now-deprecated aluminum branch wiring for a window in the mid-1970s, or with GFCI gaps in kitchens and bathrooms that predate the 1996 code requirement.
housing_patterns.symptoms: outlets that worked yesterday and don't today, intermittent power loss to one room, GFCIs that trip the moment a hairdryer plugs in.

housing_patterns.title: 2000s-2020s townhomes & newer detached
housing_patterns.neighborhood_examples: Tysons-edge, Wolf Trap area, newer subdivisions
housing_patterns.context_paragraph: Newer homes are not exempt. AFCI breakers (the arc-fault interrupters required by modern code) are sensitive by design and trip on any noisy load. Smart-home wiring done by the previous owner's "handy friend" can leave neutral wires bonded incorrectly.
housing_patterns.symptoms: failed dimmers, dead three-way switches, outlets that test fine but won't hold a plug.

outlet-installation.summary: Replace two-prong outlets with grounded three-prong or GFCI
outlet-installation.body: Many 1950s-1970s Vienna homes (Vienna Woods, Country Club Hills) still have original ungrounded two-prong outlets. A GFCI outlet can be installed as a safe replacement even without a ground wire — it provides shock protection and satisfies code. We test each outlet and recommend GFCI or full grounding depending on your wiring.

outlet-installation.summary: Add outlets to a room that only has one or two
outlet-installation.body: Older Vienna ranches and split-levels were built with 1-2 outlets per room. A home office or living room needs 4-6. We run new wire from the nearest circuit or pull a dedicated line from the panel, depending on the load. Attic and crawl space access in most Vienna homes makes the wire run straightforward.

outlet-installation.summary: GFCI upgrade for kitchen, bathroom, or garage outlets
outlet-installation.body: The 2023 NEC expanded kitchen GFCI requirements to ALL receptacles — not just countertop outlets. Most pre-2023 Vienna kitchens have 1-2 GFCI outlets at the counter and standard outlets everywhere else. We upgrade the full kitchen in one visit, plus bathrooms, garage, laundry, and outdoor outlets.

outlet-installation.summary: Dedicated circuit for a home office
outlet-installation.body: Vienna's work-from-home population is significant. A computer, two monitors, a printer, and a desk lamp on a shared bedroom circuit will trip the breaker when the space heater kicks on. We run a dedicated 20-amp circuit from the panel to the office so your equipment runs without interruptions.

outlet-installation.summary: Install a 220V/240V outlet for a dryer, range, or welder
outlet-installation.body: Switching from gas to electric for a dryer or range requires a new 240V outlet and a dedicated circuit from the panel. We install NEMA 14-30 (dryer), NEMA 14-50 (range or welder), or NEMA 6-50 (welder) outlets with the correct wire gauge and breaker size. Common in Vienna garage workshops too.

outlet-installation.summary: Smart switch or dimmer switch installation
outlet-installation.body: Replacing a toggle switch with a Lutron Caseta, TP-Link Kasa, or other smart switch requires a neutral wire — and many pre-1990 Vienna homes don't have one at the switch box. We check the wiring, install the switch, and make sure LED dimmers are compatible with your fixtures. Three-way and four-way switch wiring is included.

smoke-alarm.summary: Battery-only smoke alarms chirping or past 10-year life
smoke-alarm.body: Most 1960s-1980s Vienna homes (Vienna Woods, Country Club Hills, Windover Heights) have standalone battery-only alarms installed decades ago. The 10-year NFPA replacement mandate means any alarm installed before 2016 is due. We replace with hardwired interconnected units so all alarms sound together — the code-required standard for renovations.

smoke-alarm.summary: Upgrading to hardwired interconnected alarms (whole house)
smoke-alarm.body: Older Vienna homes typically have non-interconnected alarms — if the downstairs alarm triggers, upstairs bedrooms hear nothing. Hardwired interconnected systems wire every alarm on one circuit. When one triggers, all sound. We run the wiring through attic and crawl access (available in most Vienna stock) and test every unit.

smoke-alarm.summary: Smoke alarm code compliance for a home sale
smoke-alarm.body: When you sell in Vienna, the buyer's inspector flags non-compliant smoke alarms — missing from bedrooms, expired units, no interconnection. Getting compliant before listing avoids last-minute delays. We assess the house, install what's needed, and give documentation for the listing agent. Vienna's dual-approval permitting (Town + County) applies if new circuits are involved.

smoke-alarm.summary: Adding carbon monoxide detectors alongside smoke alarms
smoke-alarm.body: Virginia code requires CO detectors on every level with a fuel-burning appliance or attached garage. Many Vienna homes have Washington Gas service for heating — that triggers the CO requirement. Combination smoke/CO units cover both in one device. We install combo units and integrate them with the existing alarm circuit.

smoke-alarm.summary: False alarms from kitchen or bathroom steam
smoke-alarm.body: Alarms near the kitchen or bathroom that trigger during cooking or showering are usually either too close (under 10 feet per NFPA guidance) or past their 10-year life with degraded nuisance resistance. We relocate and replace with modern photoelectric units that are more resistant to cooking particles while still meeting code placement requirements.

smoke-alarm.summary: Post-renovation alarm placement (finished basement, new bedroom)
smoke-alarm.body: A finished basement, attic conversion, or added bedroom in a Vienna colonial triggers code requirements for smoke alarms in the new space. We add hardwired alarms in the new areas and integrate them with the existing system. Common in Hunter Mill and Southwest Vienna homes adding livable basement space.

troubleshooting.summary: Lights flicker when the AC or fridge kicks on
troubleshooting.body: Voltage drop. Often a loose neutral at the meter base or a damaged feeder. Common in older Vienna Woods and Country Club Hills homes built before 1980 — the service entrance is reaching the end of its life. Worth diagnosing soon: persistent voltage drops shorten the life of every motor in your house.

troubleshooting.summary: A breaker keeps tripping (more than once a week)
troubleshooting.body: The breaker is doing its job — something's wrong upstream. Usually an overloaded circuit (new microwave + toaster on the same line), a short in a wall outlet, or a failed breaker itself. We trace which of the three in 30-60 minutes.

troubleshooting.summary: An outlet or switch plate feels warm to the touch
troubleshooting.body: Stop using the circuit and call us today. Heat at a connection means resistance, and resistance behind drywall is how house fires start. Most common in 1970s-1990s Hunter Mill colonials with original wire-nut splices in junction boxes.

troubleshooting.summary: You smell burning plastic or "hot" electrical odor
troubleshooting.body: Treat this as urgent. Shut off the breaker for the affected area if you can identify it. We triage these calls to the earliest slot — typically same-day in Vienna. The cause is almost always overheated insulation at a loose connection.

troubleshooting.summary: Half your house has power, half doesn't
troubleshooting.body: An open neutral at the service entrance. Serious condition — it can fluctuate voltage between 50V and 200V and damage electronics. We test each leg of the panel and identify the failure point. Often a utility-side issue but we confirm before calling Dominion Energy.

troubleshooting.summary: Your EV charger throttles, trips, or warms the outlet
troubleshooting.body: EV charging puts continuous 30-50 amp draw on circuits that older Vienna homes weren't designed for. The cause is usually upstream of the charger — a feeder, a breaker, or a connection that can't sustain the load. Common in Wolf Trap and Tysons-edge homes where owners added a Level 2 charger to a pre-2010 panel.

most_common_problem_paragraph.outlet-installation: Two projects dominate. In 1950s-1970s homes (Vienna Woods, Country Club Hills), homeowners need more outlets — the original 1-2 per room can't handle modern life — plus GFCI upgrades in kitchens and bathrooms that predate the code requirement. In 1970s-1990s colonials (Hunter Mill, Vienna proper), the most common call is for dedicated circuits for home offices and GFCI upgrades to meet the 2023 NEC kitchen expansion.
most_common_problem_paragraph.troubleshooting: Two patterns dominate. In 1950s-1970s homes (Vienna Woods, Country Club Hills), the most common issue is circuit overload from modern appliances on original circuits. In 1970s-1990s homes (Hunter Mill, Vienna proper), the most common issue is intermittent power loss from aging connections in outlet boxes, panels, or junction boxes hidden in walls.
most_common_problem_paragraph.smoke-alarm: Two patterns dominate. In 1960s-1980s homes (Vienna Woods, Country Club Hills, Windover Heights), the original battery-only smoke alarms are past their 10-year life and not interconnected — when one triggers, the others stay silent. In homes being sold or renovated, the buyer's inspector flags missing, expired, or non-interconnected alarms, and the owner needs to get compliant before closing.

specific_problems_neighborhood_phrase.outlet-installation: Vienna's median home was built in 1971 — before GFCI requirements, before modern circuit loads, and before anyone needed six outlets in a bedroom.
specific_problems_neighborhood_phrase.troubleshooting: Vienna has more EV drivers per square mile than most Fairfax County zip codes.
specific_problems_neighborhood_phrase.smoke-alarm: Vienna's median home was built in 1971 — well before interconnected hardwired smoke alarms became the code standard. Most original alarms are standalone, battery-only, and past their 10-year replacement date.
